title: Primary sources for regional land-management scenarios
scope: Public source-only research for the existing InVEST3.20 profile workflow

sources.title: InVEST 3.20.0 Nutrient Delivery Ratio
sources.locator: Data Needs: Biophysical Table; model equations; limitations
sources.findings: load_n/load_p use kg/ha/year. Application-rate loads are internally multiplied by (1-eff); measured-runoff loads enter directly. eff_n/eff_p are maximum retention proportions; crit_len_n/crit_len_p are retention lengths in metres. Subsurface nitrogen has a separate pathway and parameters. The model does not represent in-stream nutrient retention.
sources.application: Preserve each saved load_type. A fertilizer-rate cut cannot be treated as a measured-runoff cut without an explicit supported conversion. A retention change on application-rate rows also changes the locally generated load. A single observed buffer removal and width cannot independently identify both maximum efficiency and critical length.

sources.title: InVEST 3.20.0 Sediment Delivery Ratio
sources.locator: RUSLE equation; connectivity equations; Biophysical Table; Data Sources
sources.findings: Annual hillslope erosion is R*K*LS*C*P. C represents cover and management and also influences connectivity; P represents support practices such as contouring, strip cropping and terracing. P=1 is the no-practice/unknown-practice reference. Gully and channel sources are outside the hillslope model.
sources.application: Keep C and P effects distinct. Do not apply the same measured erosion reduction to both. An observed plot sediment ratio is not automatically a calibrated C ratio or a watershed sediment-export ratio.

sources.title: Wischmeier and Smith 1978: USDA Agriculture Handbook 537
sources.locator: Printed page 35, Table 13 (PDF page 41; zero-based page 40); footnote corrected in PDF page65 errata
sources.scope: Historical USLE contouring support factors, not local RUSLE 2 calibration
sources.findings: Table 13 specifies slope-dependent absolute P factors and maximum field slope lengths. Values and lengths are retained in contouring-p-targets.csv. The table is conditional on the described contouring setting; concentrated-flow depressions require suitable protection. Its length extension footnote requires regularly greater than 50% residue cover after crop planting.
sources.application: Use an absolute target, not another multiplication by the target. Match actual field gradient, length and practice. Do not interpolate the printed slope bands or infer field length from raster cell size. The optional 25% length extension is not applied here. These choices are not uncertainty bounds.

sources.title: USDA NRCS RUSLE 2 Handbook
sources.locator: RUSLE 2 input databases and management/support-practice guidance
sources.findings: RUSLE 2 uses climate, soil, management and support-practice descriptions; locally appropriate input databases and agronomic guidance matter.
sources.application: Prefer an actual field-specific RUSLE 2 management/support-practice selection when available. Retain its version and source. A generic NLCD class does not establish crop rotation, tillage, contouring or slope-length compliance.

sources.title: Raczkowski et al. 2009: Piedmont tillage, runoff and erosion
sources.locator: Methods pp 53–54; results p 57; Figure 6 p 59
sources.scope: Greensboro, North Carolina Piedmont; Mecklenburg/Enon soils; 1995–2001
sources.findings: Six years of replicated corn/soybean plots under natural rainfall compared conventional tillage with no-till. Slopes were 3.8–6.2%; no winter cover crop was grown. Mean annual soil loss was 74.7 versus 2.6 Mg/ha/year, respectively; mean runoff was 33% lower under no-till. A few extreme storms dominated conventional-tillage losses.
sources.application: Use the measured erosion response as a site-specific benchmark. It is not a direct C parameter, a nutrient-reduction coefficient, a prediction interval, or validation for a different watershed.

sources.title: Endale et al. 2019: Tillage under fixed and variable rainfall
sources.scope: Watkinsville, Georgia Southern Piedmont; Cecil soil; corn plots
sources.findings: With fixed-rate simulated rainfall, sediment loss was 919 g under conventional tillage versus 82 g under no-till. The variable-rate experiment found no significant treatment difference in sediment. No-till had greater ammonium/nitrate loads in both years and greater dissolved-reactive/total-P loads in 2005.
sources.application: Keep nutrient and sediment scenarios separate. Event-scale benefits are not annual export coefficients; the results do not support a universal nutrient benefit from no-till.

sources.title: Endale et al. 2010: Long-term tillage and poultry-litter systems
sources.locator: Interpretive Summary and Technical Abstract; 14-year study
sources.findings: No-till decreased runoff but increased drainage. Winter rye reduced nitrate leaching relative to absent/legume cover. Nitrogen-based poultry-litter application accumulated soil phosphorus, and no-till with litter increased dissolved-P concentrations. Six of 14 years were drought years.
sources.application: Do not substitute subsurface nitrate evidence for total surface N or concentration change for annual load change. No numeric annual N/P reduction interval is extracted from this author summary. The USDA citation contains a DOI typo; the DOI field records the publication identifier separately.

sources.title: Butler et al. 2008: Grassland aeration and phosphorus export
sources.locator: Technical Abstract; Journal of Environmental Quality 37:1279–1287
sources.scope: Cecil soil, mixed fescue/bermudagrass,8–12% slopes; rainfall simulation
sources.findings: Core aeration with broiler litter reduced measured total-Kjeldahl-P export 55%, total dissolved P 62% and dissolved reactive P 61% versus controls. Manure targeted 30 kg P/ha and rainfall simulation was 85 mm/hour; response depended on compaction and treatment.
sources.application: These are distinct event-scale P fractions. They do not establish an annual total-P load multiplier, a retention efficiency or a critical length. Do not add fractions together.

sources.title: Vellidis et al. 2003: Restored riparian wetland nutrient transport
sources.scope: Georgia Coastal Plain; fertilized/manured pasture; restored three-zone buffer averaging 38 m
sources.findings: Annual mass-balance estimates retained/removed 59% of incoming TN and 66% of TP across the buffer system. The site included grass, planted pines and hardwoods, with preferential subsurface pathways.
sources.application: Useful buffer-performance context, with a physiographic transfer limitation for Piedmont sites. Whole-system removal is not native maximum eff; mean buffer width is not crit_len. Do not use these two observations as independent NDR parameter estimates or apply the removal again to loads.

sources.title: Osmond, Gatiboni and Rivers 2023: Nitrogen Loss Estimation Worksheet
sources.findings: The framework applies cover-crop credits to its subsurface-N pool: rye/triticale 15%, oats/barley 10%, wheat 5%, subject to planting/termination timing. It explicitly distinguishes the accounting endpoint from edge-of-field or stream loading.
sources.application: Retain as regional practice context, not a direct InVEST total-load or maximum-retention coefficient. NLEW accounting credits are not confidence bounds for measured annual runoff.
